subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 reading-analysis task on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Choosing how to read: skimming, scanning and close reading
Understanding and critical reading: inference and deduction
Identifying and interpreting themes, ideas and information
Analysing a writer's language and its effect
Analysing form and structure, including sentence structure and tone
Recognising the conventions of different text types
Supporting a point with evidence using PEE and embedded quotation

questions.lo: Choosing how to read: skimming, scanning and close reading
questions.q: You want to get the general gist of a three-page article in under a minute. Which reading mode should you use?
questions.explain: Skimming means reading quickly over headings, first lines and key words to grasp the overall idea (the gist) without reading every word.

questions.lo: Choosing how to read: skimming, scanning and close reading
questions.q: A revision guide asks you to 'analyse how the writer creates a tense mood' in one paragraph. Which reading mode fits the task best?
questions.explain: Analysing how meaning is made needs slow, careful close reading of the short section so you can examine specific word choices and structure.

questions.lo: Understanding and critical reading: inference and deduction
questions.q: What is an inference?
options: A fact stated directly on the page
A sensible conclusion worked out from clues in the text
A summary of the whole story
Your personal opinion of the author
questions.explain: An inference is 'reading between the lines' — a reasonable conclusion drawn from evidence in the text, not something the writer states outright.

questions.lo: Understanding and critical reading: inference and deduction
questions.q: Read: "Tom slammed the door and refused to look at anyone." What is the best inference?
options: Tom is feeling angry or upset
questions.explain: Slamming the door and refusing eye contact are clues that imply anger or upset. The other options aren't supported by any detail in the sentence.

questions.lo: Understanding and critical reading: inference and deduction
questions.q: A classmate writes: "She is clearly nervous, it's obvious." What is the main weakness of this answer?
options: It gives no evidence from the text to support the inference
It names a technique but not its effect
questions.explain: An inference must be backed by evidence. Saying it is 'obvious' proves nothing — you should point to the exact word or detail that shows nervousness.

questions.lo: Identifying and interpreting themes, ideas and information
questions.q: Which of these is a theme rather than a plot point?
options: A girl finds a lost dog in the park
questions.explain: A theme is a big, recurring idea such as courage. The other options describe individual events (plot), not the underlying idea the text explores.

questions.lo: Identifying and interpreting themes, ideas and information
questions.q: Across a story, characters keep forgiving each other and rebuilding trust after arguments. Which theme fits best?
questions.explain: The repeated pattern of forgiving and rebuilding trust points to the theme of forgiveness. The others are single details, not the recurring idea.

questions.lo: Analysing a writer's language and its effect
questions.q: "The wind whispered through the trees." Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Giving the wind the human action of whispering is personification — a non-human thing is described as if it can behave like a person.

questions.lo: Analysing a writer's language and its effect
questions.q: "Her hands were as cold as ice." Which technique is this?
questions.explain: It compares her hands to ice using the word 'as', which makes it a simile. A metaphor would say the hands WERE ice, without 'like' or 'as'.

questions.lo: Analysing a writer's language and its effect
questions.q: "The city was a hungry monster, swallowing everyone who arrived." Which answer names the technique AND its effect?
options: Simile — it compares the city to arrivals
Metaphor — it makes the city seem dangerous and overwhelming, as if it devours people
Alliteration — it repeats the letter c
questions.explain: Calling the city a 'hungry monster' is a metaphor, and its effect is to make the city feel dangerous and overwhelming. Marks come from naming the effect, not just the device.

questions.lo: Analysing a writer's language and its effect
questions.q: Which response best explains the EFFECT of a technique, rather than just labelling it?
options: There is a simile in line two.
The metaphor 'a sea of faces' makes the crowd feel huge and overwhelming.
questions.explain: Only this option explains what the metaphor makes the reader picture or feel (a huge, overwhelming crowd). The others merely name the device.

questions.lo: Analysing form and structure, including sentence structure and tone
questions.q: After several long sentences a writer adds: "Then, nothing." What is the likely effect of this short sentence?
options: It confuses the reader for no reason
It creates emphasis, shock or a sudden pause
It shows the writer ran out of words
It changes the text into a poem
questions.explain: A short, blunt sentence after longer ones stands out and creates emphasis or a dramatic pause — a deliberate structural choice.

questions.lo: Analysing form and structure, including sentence structure and tone
questions.q: What does the 'tone' of a text refer to?
options: The writer's attitude or mood, shown through word choice
questions.explain: Tone is the writer's attitude or feeling towards the subject — for example playful, angry or formal — communicated mainly through word choice.

questions.lo: Recognising the conventions of different text types
questions.q: A text has stage directions in brackets and character names before each line of speech. Which text type is it?
questions.explain: Stage directions and character names before spoken lines are conventions of a play script — features you expect from that text type.

questions.lo: Recognising the conventions of different text types
questions.q: Which feature is a typical convention of a formal non-fiction article rather than a personal diary?
options: Informative subheadings and factual, impersonal language
questions.explain: Subheadings and factual, impersonal language are conventions of formal non-fiction. A diary is private, personal and full of feelings.

questions.lo: Making critical comparisons between texts
questions.q: Which sentence makes a genuine critical comparison of two texts?
options: Text A is good. Text B is also there.
Text A describes the sea as 'calm', whereas Text B calls it a 'raging beast', so A feels peaceful while B feels dangerous.
Both texts contain words and sentences.
questions.explain: A critical comparison examines the same feature (how each describes the sea) across both texts, uses a contrast word ('whereas') and supports each side with evidence.

questions.lo: Making critical comparisons between texts
questions.q: Which linking word is most useful for showing a DIFFERENCE between two texts?
questions.explain: 'Whereas' signals a contrast, so it is ideal for pointing out a difference. 'Similarly', 'likewise' and 'both' signal similarities instead.

questions.lo: Supporting a point with evidence using PEE and embedded quotation
questions.q: In the PEE structure, what do the three letters stand for?
questions.explain: PEE stands for Point (a clear claim), Evidence (a short quotation) and Explain (how the quotation proves the point or its effect).

questions.lo: Supporting a point with evidence using PEE and embedded quotation
questions.q: Text: "The soldier trudged through the endless mud." Which sentence embeds a quotation best?
options: The writer talks about a soldier and some mud.
The word 'endless' makes the mud feel never-ending and hints at the soldier's exhaustion.
The quotation is 'The soldier trudged through the endless mud.'
Mud is messy, so the soldier must be unhappy.
questions.explain: It embeds a single key word ('endless') smoothly into the sentence and explains its effect. Quoting the whole line or giving no quote at all is weaker.

questions.lo: Supporting a point with evidence using PEE and embedded quotation
questions.q: What is the main problem with using a very long quotation in a PEE paragraph?
options: It takes up space without focusing on the key word you want to explain
It automatically makes the point wrong
questions.explain: Long quotations bury the important word. Embedding a short quote keeps the focus on the exact language you are analysing and its effect.
